Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) -- Civilian deaths in Afghanistan have risen sharply in the past year, largely due to more Taliban attacks and roadside bombings, U.N. officials said Sunday. NATO soldiers sit in their vehicle in an Afghan province freed from Taliban forces. Afghan civilian deaths jumped from 430 in the first six months of 2007 to 698 so far this year, an increase of 60 percent, said John Holmes, the United Nations undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs. "It is clear that the international military forces are making every effort to minimize civilian casualties," Holmes said. "Nevertheless, these problems are still there, and we need to deal with them and make sure that the safety of civilians comes first and international humanitarian law is respected," he said. Taliban insurgents forces have shifted from direct attacks on international troops toward the use of "civilian-blind" measures such as roadside bombings and suicide attacks, said Aleem Siddique, a spokesman for the U.N. Assistance Mission in Afghanistan. At the same time, he said, civilian deaths blamed on government forces and U.S. and NATO troops has declined in the first six months of 2008, largely due to pressure from Afghan President Hamid Karzai. About 60 percent of civilian deaths in 2008 are blamed on anti-government forces, up from less than half in 2007. Increased Taliban attacks on aid projects also have left 78 of Afghanistan's 398 districts off-limits to relief workers, Siddique said. "Increasingly, we're seeing targets of schools, of radio stations, of health clinics -- all in an effort to halt progress and keep people in fear," he said. A total of 565 aid convoys came under attack in 2007, with hundreds of tons of food hijacked. As recently as Sunday, a convoy of 100 tons of food aid came under attack outside Kandahar, with several trucks burned and looted, he said. "Thankfully, we're not getting any report of death or injuries," he said. Afghanistan is the original front in the "war on terrorism," which was launched after al Qaeda's September 11, 2001, attacks on New York and Washington. A U.S.-led invasion after the attacks pushed out the Taliban, which had allowed al Qaeda to operate from its territory, but the Islamic fundamentalist militia has regrouped along and across the mountainous border with Pakistan. Coinciding with the rise in civilian deaths in 2008 is an increase in attacks on American and allied forces, which are up 40 percent since last year . The death toll of U.S. and allied troops in Afghanistan in June also climbed to more than 40, making it the deadliest month since the war began. An explosion in southern Afghanistan killed a British soldier serving with NATO on Saturday, the British Defense Ministry said Sunday. The soldier died when he was struck by a mine in Lashkar Gah, the capital city of Helmand province, the ministry said. He and his unit were investigating a report of a rocket-propelled grenade attack on a civilian aircraft at a nearby airfield, it said. "When investigating this, they dismounted their vehicles and what is believed to have been a legacy anti-Personnel mine detonated, killing the soldier instantly," the ministry statement said. Most of the soldiers serving in Helmand are British. Helmand province is Afghanistan's top poppy-producing region and a major front in the war against the Taliban. Provincial authorities there have blamed militants for a spate of recent deadly attacks. NATO and Afghan force operations kept the insurgency down in 2007 by killing or capturing key leaders and clearing out Taliban safe havens, but a Pentagon report issued last week predicted the Taliban would be back in 2008.

Afghan civilian deaths rose from 430 in the first six months of 2007 to 698 so far this year—an increase of 60 percent—said John Holmes, the United Nations undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs.

At the same time, Siddique said, civilian deaths attributed to government forces and U.S. and NATO troops declined in the first six months of 2008, largely because of pressure from Afghan President Hamid Karzai.

Increased Taliban attacks on aid projects have also left 78 of Afghanistan’s 398 districts inaccessible to relief workers, Siddique said.

“Increasingly, we are seeing schools, radio stations, and health clinics targeted—all in an effort to halt progress and keep people in fear,” he said.

A total of 565 aid convoys came under attack in 2007, with hundreds of tons of food hijacked. As recently as Sunday, a convoy carrying 100 tons of food aid came under attack outside Kandahar, with several trucks burned and looted, Siddique said.

“Thankfully, we are not receiving any reports of deaths or injuries,” he said.

Afghanistan is the original front in the “war on terrorism,” launched after al Qaeda’s September 11, 2001, attacks on New York and Washington. A U.S.-led invasion following the attacks ousted the Taliban, which had allowed al Qaeda to operate from Afghan territory. However, the Islamic fundamentalist militia has since regrouped along and across the mountainous border with Pakistan.

Coinciding with the rise in civilian deaths in 2008 is an increase in attacks on American and allied forces, which are up 40 percent from last year. The death toll among U.S. and allied troops in Afghanistan in June also climbed to more than 40, making it the deadliest month since the war began.

An explosion in southern Afghanistan killed a British soldier serving with NATO on Saturday, the British Defense Ministry said Sunday. The soldier died after being struck by a mine in Lashkar Gah, the capital of Helmand province, the ministry said.

He and his unit were investigating a report of a rocket-propelled grenade attack on a civilian aircraft at a nearby airfield, the ministry said.

“While investigating this, they dismounted their vehicles, and what is believed to have been a legacy anti-personnel mine detonated, killing the soldier instantly,” the ministry statement said.

Most of the soldiers serving in Helmand are British. Helmand province is Afghanistan’s leading poppy-producing region and a major front in the war against the Taliban. Provincial authorities there have blamed militants for a series of recent deadly attacks.

NATO and Afghan force operations suppressed the insurgency in 2007 by killing or capturing key leaders and clearing Taliban safe havens, but a Pentagon report issued last week predicted that the Taliban would return in 2008.

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) — The number of Afghan civilians killed has climbed steeply over the last year, mainly because of increased Taliban assaults and roadside bomb attacks, United Nations officials said Sunday.

NATO troops were seen seated inside a vehicle in an Afghan province that had been cleared of Taliban fighters.

John Holmes, the U.N. undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs, said civilian fatalities in Afghanistan rose from 430 during the first half of 2007 to 698 in the same period this year, a 60 percent increase.

Holmes said international forces are clearly trying hard to reduce civilian casualties. Even so, he added, the issue remains serious and must be addressed, with civilian protection treated as the top priority and international humanitarian law upheld.

Aleem Siddique, a spokesman for the U.N. Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, said Taliban insurgents have moved away from directly confronting foreign troops and are increasingly relying on tactics that do not distinguish between civilians and combatants, including suicide attacks and roadside bombs.

Siddique also said that deaths attributed to Afghan government forces and to U.S. and NATO troops fell during the first six months of 2008, largely because of pressure from Afghan President Hamid Karzai.

Anti-government forces are being blamed for roughly 60 percent of civilian deaths in 2008, compared with less than half in 2007.

The rise in Taliban attacks on aid operations has also made 78 of Afghanistan’s 398 districts inaccessible to relief workers, Siddique said.

He said schools, radio stations and health clinics are increasingly being targeted as part of an effort to stop development and keep the population afraid.

In 2007, 565 aid convoys were attacked, and hundreds of tons of food were seized. Siddique said that as recently as Sunday, a convoy carrying 100 tons of food assistance was attacked outside Kandahar, where several trucks were burned and looted.

He said there had fortunately been no reports of deaths or injuries from that incident.

Afghanistan was the first battlefield in the “war on terrorism,” launched after al Qaeda carried out the September 11, 2001, attacks on New York and Washington. Following those attacks, a U.S.-led invasion drove the Taliban from power. The Taliban had permitted al Qaeda to operate from Afghan territory, but the hard-line Islamist militia later regrouped in and around the rugged border region with Pakistan.

Alongside the 2008 increase in civilian deaths, attacks on U.S. and allied troops have also risen, up 40 percent from the previous year.

More than 40 American and allied service members were killed in Afghanistan in June, making it the deadliest month since the conflict began.

The British Defense Ministry said Sunday that a British soldier serving with NATO was killed Saturday in an explosion in southern Afghanistan.

According to the ministry, the soldier died after being hit by a mine in Lashkar Gah, the capital of Helmand province. He and his unit had been looking into a report that a civilian aircraft had been attacked with a rocket-propelled grenade at a nearby airfield.

The ministry said the troops had left their vehicles while investigating when what was believed to be an old anti-personnel mine exploded, killing the soldier immediately.

Most troops deployed in Helmand are British. The province is Afghanistan’s leading poppy-producing area and a key battleground in the fight against the Taliban.

Officials in the province have accused militants of carrying out a recent series of deadly attacks.

NATO and Afghan military operations suppressed the insurgency in 2007 by killing or capturing important leaders and eliminating Taliban sanctuaries. However, a Pentagon report released last week forecast that the Taliban would return in 2008.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article from Kabul about U.N. officials reporting a sharp rise in Afghan civilian deaths in 2008, including Taliban roadside bombings, aid convoy attacks, NATO casualties, and comments from John Holmes and Aleem Siddique.
counterfactuals.output:
**KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN-style)** — Civilian deaths in Afghanistan rose sharply in 2008, driven largely by Taliban roadside bombings, suicide attacks and expanding fighting between insurgents and international forces, U.N. officials said.

The United Nations said more than 2,000 Afghan civilians were killed during the year, a significant increase from 2007 and a grim sign of the worsening security situation across the country. U.N. officials attributed the majority of the deaths to anti-government militants, including the Taliban, who increasingly relied on improvised explosive devices, or IEDs, in attacks on roads, markets and government targets.

Roadside bombs were among the deadliest tactics, often striking civilian vehicles as well as military convoys. The Taliban also stepped up attacks on aid convoys and humanitarian workers, making it harder for relief agencies to operate in areas already suffering from poverty, displacement and food shortages.

John Holmes, the U.N. emergency relief coordinator, said the rise in civilian casualties underscored the growing toll of the conflict on ordinary Afghans.

“The security situation has deteriorated significantly,” Holmes said, warning that civilians were paying the highest price as insurgent attacks spread and military operations intensified.

U.N. spokesman Aleem Siddique said humanitarian access had become increasingly difficult, with aid workers facing intimidation, kidnappings and deadly attacks.

“Afghans need assistance, but reaching them is becoming more dangerous,” Siddique said. He said attacks on aid convoys and relief personnel were disrupting deliveries of food, medicine and other supplies to vulnerable communities.

The violence also took a heavy toll on international forces. NATO and U.S.-led coalition troops suffered one of their deadliest years since the 2001 invasion, as insurgents expanded operations beyond traditional strongholds in the south and east. Foreign troops were increasingly targeted by roadside bombs and ambushes, while Afghan civilians were often caught in the crossfire or killed in militant attacks aimed at security forces.

U.N. officials said insurgent groups were responsible for the largest share of civilian deaths, but they also cited casualties caused by airstrikes and ground operations involving Afghan and international forces. The issue has become a major source of tension between President Hamid Karzai’s government and Western military commanders.

Karzai has repeatedly called on NATO forces to do more to prevent civilian deaths, saying such incidents undermine public support for the Afghan government and the international mission.

The U.N. said the rising casualty figures reflected a broader deterioration in the war, with violence spreading into previously calmer regions and humanitarian workers facing unprecedented risks.

Officials warned that unless civilians are better protected and aid groups are given safe access, Afghanistan’s humanitarian crisis could deepen further.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a full wire-service report on civilian casualties in Afghanistan increasing from 430 in early 2007 to 698 in early 2008, with background on the Taliban insurgency, attacks on aid workers, and recent British military deaths in Helmand province.
counterfactuals.output:
**Civilian casualties rise sharply in Afghanistan as insurgency intensifies**

**KABUL, Afghanistan, July 2008** — Civilian casualties in Afghanistan rose sharply in the first months of 2008, climbing from 430 during the same period a year earlier to 698, according to figures cited by international officials, underscoring the growing toll of the conflict as Taliban-led insurgents expand attacks and foreign forces press operations in the country’s south and east.

The increase reflects a deteriorating security environment more than six years after the Taliban were driven from power by a U.S.-led invasion in late 2001. Despite the presence of tens of thousands of NATO and U.S. troops, insurgents have regrouped in border areas, especially along the frontier with Pakistan, and have mounted increasingly deadly attacks against Afghan government targets, foreign troops, police, aid organizations and civilians.

International officials and human rights groups have repeatedly warned that civilians are being caught between insurgent tactics — including suicide bombings, roadside bombs and attacks in populated areas — and military operations by Afghan and foreign forces, including airstrikes and ground assaults.

The Taliban insurgency has intensified across much of southern and eastern Afghanistan, with Helmand, Kandahar, Uruzgan, Zabul, Khost and Paktika among the most volatile provinces. Insurgents have relied heavily on improvised explosive devices, ambushes and suicide attacks, tactics that have caused mounting civilian casualties while also inflicting losses on NATO-led forces.

Aid agencies have also come under increasing threat. Humanitarian workers, once able to operate in many parts of Afghanistan with relative freedom, have faced kidnappings, ambushes and killings as insurgents target those seen as supporting the Afghan government or foreign presence. The attacks have forced some organizations to scale back operations, suspend travel or withdraw staff from insecure districts, reducing assistance to communities already suffering from poverty, drought and displacement.

The worsening violence has been particularly severe in Helmand province, a major center of the insurgency and Afghanistan’s opium trade. British forces, deployed there as part of NATO’s International Security Assistance Force, have faced some of the heaviest fighting of the war. Recent British military deaths in Helmand have added to concerns in London over the cost of the mission and the resilience of Taliban fighters in the province.

Helmand has been the scene of repeated battles around towns, irrigation districts and key roads, with insurgents using the province’s terrain, drug networks and porous links to Pakistan to sustain operations. British troops have been involved in efforts to secure population centers, train Afghan forces and disrupt Taliban supply routes, but gains have often proved difficult to hold without a stronger Afghan government presence.

Afghan President Hamid Karzai has urged international forces to do more to prevent civilian deaths, warning that casualties undermine public support for the government and foreign troops. NATO commanders say insurgents deliberately endanger civilians by using homes, mosques and villages as cover, but they have also acknowledged the need to reduce harm from military operations.

The rise from 430 civilian casualties in early 2007 to 698 in early 2008 points to a conflict that has grown more complex and more lethal for ordinary Afghans. With insurgent attacks spreading and aid operations increasingly constrained, officials warn that the humanitarian situation could worsen unless security improves and greater protections are put in place for civilians.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a news story dated from Kabul summarizing U.N. concerns that Taliban tactics are causing more civilian deaths in Afghanistan, while casualties blamed on Afghan, U.S., and NATO forces have declined.
counterfactuals.output:
**KABUL, Afghanistan, Aug. 10** — The United Nations warned Tuesday that Taliban tactics are driving a sharp rise in civilian casualties in Afghanistan, even as deaths and injuries attributed to Afghan government forces and their U.S. and NATO allies have declined.

In a new report, the U.N. mission in Afghanistan said insurgent attacks — particularly roadside bombs, suicide strikes and targeted killings — were responsible for the vast majority of civilian casualties. The report said anti-government fighters caused about three-quarters of recorded civilian deaths and injuries in the first half of the year, a significant increase from the same period a year earlier.

U.N. officials said the growing use of improvised explosive devices, often planted on roads or in crowded areas, has been especially deadly because the weapons frequently strike civilians rather than military targets. The report also cited an increase in assassinations and executions of local officials, tribal elders, religious figures and Afghans accused of supporting the government.

By contrast, the U.N. said civilian casualties blamed on pro-government forces — including Afghan troops, U.S. forces and NATO units — fell, reflecting tighter rules on airstrikes and battlefield operations intended to reduce harm to civilians. Civilian deaths from air operations, once a major source of public anger, have dropped substantially, the report said.

Still, the overall toll on civilians has continued to climb as fighting spreads and insurgents intensify attacks. U.N. officials urged the Taliban and other armed groups to stop using tactics that fail to distinguish between civilians and combatants, saying such methods may violate international humanitarian law.

The issue remains politically sensitive for the Afghan government and its Western backers, who have struggled to maintain public support while fighting a resilient insurgency. Civilian casualties have long fueled anger against foreign forces, but the latest U.N. findings suggest insurgent violence is now the primary cause of harm to Afghan civilians.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a CNN article about the worsening security situation in Afghanistan: rising civilian deaths, more attacks on aid convoys and schools, Taliban use of suicide attacks and roadside bombs, and increased casualties among U.S. and allied troops.
counterfactuals.output:
**Draft news article for CNN-style publication**

**Security deteriorates in Afghanistan as civilians, aid workers and foreign troops face mounting violence**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*Kabul, Afghanistan — [Date]*

Afghanistan’s security situation is worsening, with civilians bearing a growing share of the violence as insurgent attacks intensify across the country, according to Afghan officials, aid groups and international military sources.

In recent weeks, attacks have struck aid convoys, schools, government offices and crowded public areas, underscoring the Taliban’s continued ability to carry out coordinated assaults despite years of counterinsurgency operations by Afghan forces and their U.S. and allied partners.

Humanitarian organizations say the violence is making it increasingly difficult to deliver food, medical supplies and other assistance to vulnerable communities, particularly in rural districts where roads are frequently targeted with roadside bombs and improvised explosive devices.

“Access is becoming more dangerous and more unpredictable,” said one aid official, who asked not to be named because of security concerns. “Convoys are being attacked, staff are being threatened, and communities that rely on assistance are the ones paying the highest price.”

Afghan authorities say civilian deaths have risen as militants increasingly use suicide bombers, car bombs and roadside explosives in populated areas. Schools have also come under attack, disrupting education for thousands of children and raising fears among families already caught between insurgents and security forces.

The Taliban has claimed responsibility for several recent attacks, saying its fighters are targeting foreign troops and Afghan government forces. But Afghan officials and human rights monitors say many of the attacks have killed or wounded civilians, including children.

The violence has also taken a heavier toll on U.S. and allied forces. Military officials have reported an increase in casualties among troops operating in volatile provinces, where patrols face ambushes, suicide attacks and hidden explosives planted along supply routes.

Roadside bombs remain one of the deadliest threats. Often buried along highways or near military and humanitarian routes, the devices can be difficult to detect and have caused significant casualties among civilians, Afghan security forces and foreign troops.

The intensifying violence comes as the Afghan government struggles to extend its authority beyond major cities. In several provinces, security forces are fighting to hold district centers while insurgents exert influence in surrounding rural areas.

Analysts say the Taliban’s tactics are designed not only to inflict casualties but also to undermine public confidence in the government and discourage international engagement.

“By attacking schools, aid convoys and key roads, insurgents are trying to demonstrate that the state cannot protect people or deliver basic services,” said [Analyst Name], a regional security expert. “The psychological impact is as important as the battlefield impact.”

Afghan officials have vowed to continue operations against insurgent networks and say additional security measures are being put in place to protect civilians, schools and aid deliveries. But humanitarian groups warn that without improved security, millions of Afghans could face reduced access to lifesaving support.

For many families, the immediate concern is survival.

“We are afraid to send our children to school, and we are afraid to travel,” said a resident of [Province/City], where recent violence has forced some families from their homes. “Every road can be dangerous. Every day we hear about another explosion.”

As civilian casualties rise and attacks spread, Afghanistan’s fragile security gains appear increasingly under threat — leaving ordinary Afghans, aid workers and troops on the front lines of a conflict with no clear end in sight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
**Breaking News: Afghanistan Violence Surges as U.N. Reports Sharp Rise in Civilian Deaths; Taliban Target Aid Projects; British NATO Soldier Killed in Helmand**

**KABUL, Afghanistan — 2008** — Afghanistan’s conflict is intensifying across much of the country, with the United Nations reporting a steep rise in civilian casualties as Taliban-led insurgents expand attacks on government targets, foreign forces, and humanitarian and reconstruction projects.

The latest U.N. casualty figures show that Afghan civilians are paying an increasingly heavy price in the seventh year of the U.S.-led war that followed the September 11, 2001, attacks. U.N. officials say civilian deaths have risen sharply compared with the previous year, with insurgent bombings, suicide attacks, assassinations, and clashes between Taliban fighters and international troops contributing to the toll.

According to U.N. reporting for 2008, more than 2,000 Afghan civilians were killed during the year — a major increase from 2007. The United Nations attributed the majority of deaths to anti-government elements, including the Taliban, while also recording significant civilian casualties caused by pro-government forces, particularly in airstrikes and combat operations involving NATO and U.S.-led coalition troops.

The casualty figures have renewed concern among Afghan officials, aid groups, and international diplomats that the war is becoming deadlier for ordinary Afghans, especially in the south and east, where insurgent activity is strongest.

## Taliban Attacks on Humanitarian and Reconstruction Projects

The Taliban and allied insurgent groups have increasingly targeted projects intended to rebuild Afghanistan’s infrastructure and support civilian life, including schools, roads, clinics, bridges, and aid convoys.

Humanitarian organizations say militants have attacked construction crews, burned schools, kidnapped workers, and threatened local communities that cooperate with the Afghan government or foreign-backed development programs. Road-building projects — critical to linking rural districts with markets, hospitals, and government services — have become frequent targets because they also improve military mobility for Afghan and NATO forces.

Aid workers warn that the violence is forcing some organizations to scale back operations or withdraw from dangerous districts, leaving vulnerable communities without health care, education, food assistance, and reconstruction support.

The attacks come as insurgents seek to undermine President Hamid Karzai’s government and portray foreign-funded development as part of the Western military campaign. In several provinces, Taliban commanders have warned Afghans not to work with international agencies or government contractors, often backing those threats with killings or abductions.

## War on Terrorism Background

Afghanistan has been at the center of the U.S.-led “war on terrorism” since late 2001, when American and allied forces invaded after the Taliban refused to hand over al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden following the September 11 attacks.

The Taliban government was quickly toppled, but its fighters regrouped in rural Afghanistan and across the border in Pakistan’s tribal areas. By 2008, the insurgency had become more organized and more lethal, using roadside bombs, suicide attacks, ambushes, and intimidation campaigns.

NATO’s International Security Assistance Force, or ISAF, has expanded its mission across Afghanistan, with troops from the United States, Britain, Canada, the Netherlands, Germany, France, and other alliance members operating alongside Afghan security forces. The south — particularly Helmand and Kandahar provinces — remains one of the most dangerous regions, with Taliban fighters battling for influence over key districts and opium-producing areas.

The United States and NATO say their forces are fighting to prevent Afghanistan from again becoming a safe haven for international terrorist groups. But rising civilian casualties and insurgent attacks have increased pressure on Afghan and Western leaders to adjust strategy, improve protection of civilians, and speed up the training of Afghan army and police units.

## British NATO Soldier Killed in Helmand

NATO officials have also confirmed the death of a British soldier serving with the alliance in Helmand province, one of the main battlegrounds of the war.

The soldier was killed during operations in the province, where British forces have been heavily engaged against Taliban fighters. Helmand has seen repeated clashes, roadside bomb attacks, and assaults on patrols as NATO and Afghan troops attempt to secure towns, roads, and rural districts.

British forces have borne a significant share of the fighting in southern Afghanistan. The United Kingdom has deployed thousands of troops to Helmand, where they work with Afghan security forces and other NATO units to counter Taliban influence and protect reconstruction efforts.

Military officials said the soldier’s family had been informed. Further details, including the soldier’s identity and unit, were expected to be released by the Ministry of Defence after next of kin notifications were complete.

## Civilian Toll Fuels Anger and Political Pressure

The U.N. figures are likely to intensify debate over the conduct of military operations in Afghanistan. Afghan President Hamid Karzai has repeatedly criticized airstrikes and night raids that result in civilian casualties, warning that such incidents damage public support for the government and foreign forces.

NATO commanders say insurgents frequently fight from populated areas, use civilians as shields, and deliberately stage attacks near homes, mosques, and schools. But human rights groups say all sides must do more to protect civilians and investigate alleged abuses.

The Taliban’s use of suicide bombings and improvised explosive devices has been especially deadly. Roadside bombs aimed at NATO or Afghan convoys often kill civilians traveling on the same roads. Suicide attacks in crowded markets, near government buildings, and at police checkpoints have also caused heavy civilian losses.

## Humanitarian Situation Worsens

Beyond the fighting, Afghanistan faces worsening humanitarian pressures. Many communities are struggling with poverty, food insecurity, weak governance, limited access to medical care, and displacement caused by combat. Aid agencies say insecurity is making it increasingly difficult to reach remote areas.

The targeting of humanitarian projects threatens one of the central promises of the international intervention: that military action would be accompanied by reconstruction and development. In areas where schools are closed, clinics attacked, and roads made unsafe, many Afghans see little improvement in daily life despite years of foreign assistance.

## Outlook

The rising death toll, attacks on aid operations, and continued NATO casualties underscore the deteriorating security situation in Afghanistan in 2008. International forces are preparing for a prolonged campaign, while insurgents appear determined to expand their reach and disrupt both military operations and civilian reconstruction.

U.N. officials and aid groups are urging all parties to protect civilians, safeguard humanitarian workers, and allow assistance to reach those in need. But with Taliban attacks increasing and foreign forces under pressure to contain the insurgency, Afghanistan remains locked in a deepening conflict with no clear end in sight.
